name: Overclock yourself
summary: On a key the unit enters a short boosted state: it moves, fires or reloads faster, hits harder or gains bonus health, for a few seconds or for as long as it keeps the boost running. Usually it pays: a slice of health when it starts, damage for every second it runs, more damage taken while boosted, a slowdown or lock-up afterwards, or slower movement in return for more damage. A free burst of speed alone is dash, and a short trade of speed or firepower for damage reduction is brace. The levers are what is boosted, what it costs and when (on use, while running, afterwards), how long it lasts, whether it can be ended early, and whether teammates can pay the cost back.
counterplay: Back off and wait it out: the boost is short, and afterwards the unit is weaker for what it paid.
Focus it while it is boosted if the boost makes it take more damage, or right after it has paid health to start.
Kill or cut off its healers: in StarCraft II, Medivac healing is what makes repeated stims affordable.
Catch it in the slump: an overused speed boost can leave it slower than normal or locked up.
Bring targets the boost doesn't help against (the Void Ray's alignment adds damage only against armoured targets), and kite a damage boost that slows its user until it ends.

other_examples.note: Trades a fixed slice of health (the Marauder pays twice as much) for several seconds of moving and firing half again faster. Using it again while it runs refreshes the time and costs health again, and it can never kill the user. Medivac healing pays the health back, so players stim just before a fight with healers behind them.
For a while the Void Ray hits armoured units and buildings harder but flies a quarter slower; it can end the alignment early to get its speed back. Against unarmoured targets it adds nothing.

sources.title: Void Ray (reached through Prismatic Alignment), Liquipedia StarCraft II Wiki

other_examples.note: A charge with a time limit: the warriors draw their blades and run faster, cutting down infantry with one stroke, and while it lasts the enemy's scout animals can't stun them; a warrior can also charge into a garrisoned building, which costs him his life. It is useless against tanks and buildings.

shooter_analogues.note: Lets a 'Mech speed up to as much as double its normal speed, but heavy use locks up its actuators: first it drops below normal speed, and pushing on can stop it entirely.

sources.title: Myomer Accelerator Signal Circuitry (MASC), MechWarrior Online Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: The heavy suit's overdrive adds a little damage and up to half again more forward speed for a limited time, but the suit takes a fifth more damage while it runs. It burns its own energy tank, can be switched off at any time, and the tank takes a while to refill.

His tactical ability costs a fixed slice of health (it can't take him below one point) for a few seconds of faster walking and sprinting, and it clears most slows. A passive slowly regrows health and the cooldown is very short, so he can stim again and again.

A free boost on a cooldown: for a few seconds he gains extra temporary health and faster firing, reloading and movement, and it refills some ammo. Its speed bonus is exempt from the game's general cap on movement-speed buffs.

player_translation.summary: A short, visible power spike on one key: for a few seconds the unit moves and fires faster or hits harder, and it pays in health, in extra damage taken or in a slump afterwards. The decision is timing: when the spike wins the fight, and when the cost loses it.
as_user: You choose the moment: just before you commit to a fight, to run down a fleeing target, or to get away.
The cost is visible and immediate (a slice of health, a hull that burns while the boost runs, a slump when it ends), so you don't boost into a fight you were losing anyway.
Healers and repairers make it sustainable: a teammate who pays back the cost lets you boost more often, as Medivacs do for stimmed Marines.
Toggle versions that burn while on give you a choice every second: keep paying for the speed, or switch off.
as_target: A boosted enemy glows and leaves a trail, and its ring shows how long the boost has left, so you can back off until it ends.
After the boost it is weaker (health spent, or slowed), which is your moment to turn on it.
If the boost makes it take more damage, focus it at once.
teammates: Healers and repairers pay back the cost; a boosted push works best with them close behind.
Squads time their boosts together for a push.
The enemy team separates the boosted unit from its healer and kites it until the window closes.
controls: Q starts a timed boost (active), switches a running boost on and off (toggle variants), or keeps it going while held (channel variants). The pattern spends one counted key.
Nothing else changes: the boost changes how fast and hard the unit acts, not which inputs it uses.
feedback: A clear boosted look from above: glow, exhaust flare, speed lines and a coloured ring.
Sound cues when it starts and ends, and a ring that empties as the time runs out.
The cost shown as it happens: the health bar drops in a distinct colour, a burning-hull effect while a toggle runs, a slump icon afterwards.
changes_from_rts: RTS players boost whole groups with healers queued behind; here one player boosts one unit, so the boost must be strong enough to feel and short enough to answer.
A boost that can kill its user (Gastroburners left on bring the Kirov down) needs a loud warning well before that point; an RTS player watches many units, a shooter player one health bar.
Keep health costs meaningful but never self-lethal outside the burn-while-on variant: Stimpack and Octane's stim both stop short of killing the user.
A free boost with only a cooldown is fine as an extra ability, but a pure burst of speed is dash, not this pattern.
Shooters cap stacked movement buffs (Overwatch has a general cap that Overload is exempted from), so boosts here need a cap too.

team_play.notes: Mostly a solo tool; teamwork comes from healers and repairers who pay back its cost, and from squads timing their boosts for one push.

notes: A timed stat modifier with hooks for start, end and cost.
Edge cases: using it again while it runs (refresh and pay again, as Stimpack does), costs that could kill, stacking with other buffs, ending it early.
Clear visual and audio states for both teams are most of the work.
Boost-and-heal loops can make the cost meaningless (Medivacs refund stims, and the Marine's Combat Shield upgrade covers the health it costs).
Damage boosts can kill targets before they can react; keep them short and visible.
Speed boosts stacked with other buffs break movement assumptions, so they need a cap.
A boosted state is easy to show from above with a glow and a ring.
Several boosts on one unit at once, or on many units in a push, can blur together; one shared boosted look per unit keeps it readable.

variants.name: Pay in health
variants.summary: Starting the boost costs a fixed slice of health for more speed and fire rate; it never kills the user, and healers can pay it back.
variants.seen_in: StarCraft II Stimpack, Apex Legends Octane's stim

variants.name: Burn while on
variants.summary: The boost eats the unit's own health every second it runs and is switched off by hand; left on too long, it destroys the unit.

variants.name: Glass overdrive
variants.summary: More damage and speed for a while, but the unit takes more damage until the boost ends or it switches it off.

variants.name: Free surge
variants.summary: No cost but a cooldown: a few seconds of bonus health with faster firing, reloading and movement.

adds_weaknesses.why: The surge is short and then on a cooldown, so enemies who back off just wait it out.

variants.name: Slump afterwards
variants.summary: A free burst of speed whose overuse locks the unit up: first slower than normal, then briefly stuck.

adds_weaknesses.why: Overusing the boost locks it up: first slower than normal, then briefly unable to move.

variants.name: Slow but strong
variants.summary: Extra damage against one kind of target while the boost lasts, but the unit moves slower; it can end the boost early to get its speed back.

adds_weaknesses.why: While boosted it moves slower, and the bonus helps only against one kind of target.

variants.name: Charge in
variants.summary: A timed rush: the unit runs faster with a deadly close-range strike and can't be stunned while it lasts, but the strike does nothing to armour.

adds_weaknesses.why: The charge swaps its gun for a close-range strike: it must reach touching distance, and the strike does nothing to vehicles or buildings.

adds_strengths.why: Can spike its speed or firepower for a few seconds to win a fight or catch a target.

adds_weaknesses.why: Every boost costs it something: health, extra damage taken, or a slump afterwards.

countered_by.why: Long-range units back off and keep shooting until the short boost runs out.
Area and burst damage finish it off after it has paid health for the boost.

open_questions: Can a health-cost boost ever kill its user? (Recommended: no, as with Stimpack and Octane's stim; only the burn-while-on toggle may, after a clear warning.)
Should healers be able to pay the cost back, or should some costs (heat, a slump) be out of healing's reach so the cost always bites?

The Kirov's Gastroburners carry the boost mobility trait, whose key stands for dash. Should the boost trait accept overclock-self as its pattern when the speed costs the unit something? (Raised by the Kirov's fit note on mobility/traits.)
As a generic stat-buff pattern, may it ever be a card's signature? (This file says no: slot extra.)

shooter_fit.reason: Cheap to build and common in shooters (Apex Legends' stim, PlanetSide 2's overdrive, Overwatch's Overload), and readable as a glow and a timer; as a generic pattern it fills out cards rather than defining them.
